Method: Survey of where quantum algorithms could affect robotics
Key result: Maps quantum ML, quantum image processing, optimization (trajectory planning, task allocation, kinematics), sensing/perception and system diagnosis to robot functions; lists open problems
Limitation: Speculative; most cited speed-ups (e.g., quantum PCA, quantum image processing) assume fault-tolerant hardware and qRAM

Method: Monograph surveying quantum mechanisms relevant to robot sensing, planning, learning and acting
Key result: Covers quantum search, quantum Markov decision processes, quantum RL, quantum sensing and control, and quantum-scale manipulation; offers a roadmap
Limitation: Predates most NISQ-era experimental work (2019 onwards)

Method: Review of quantum robotics: architectures, perception and robot–environment interaction
Key result: Covers quantum path planning, quantum-inspired inverse kinematics, quantum RL navigation, QML, quantum sensors, multi-robot coordination, quantum affective computing, quantum image processing and quantum-secure communication
Limitation: Broad and largely descriptive; limited critical assessment of hardware feasibility

Method: Review of 107 contributions on QML for robotics
Key result: Organises the field into QRL for navigation/control, quantum search and path planning, quantum-enhanced localization and mapping, quantum optimization for IK and task allocation, and multi-robot coordination
Limitation: QML-centerd; limited treatment of sensing, cognition and deployment latency

Method: Systematic review guided by four research questions; robotics tasks recast as optimization, search, sampling and linear-algebra problems
Key result: Covers annealing and variational control, Grover-type search and quantum-inspired sampling, QML for perception and RL, and hardware/latency constraints
Limitation: Preprint

Method: Brief survey of quantum-oriented control: QNNs, QML, QPSO, quantum RL, distributed NISQ and hybrid approaches
Key result: Maps quantum-assisted adaptive control, trajectory planning and optimization methods
Limitation: Short conference review; much of the covered work is quantum-inspired

Method: Narrative review of quantum computing principles and applications in robotics, AI, data mining and image processing
Key result: Highlights integration needs and scale-up challenges
Limitation: Descriptive; lower-impact venue

Robotic task: Quantum robot concept: a mobile quantum system with an onboard quantum computer that interacts with its environment
Method: Formal model of quantum robots and the environments they act in
Key result: Introduces the quantum robot and describes how it can carry out tasks through interactions with its environment
Limitation: Theoretical; robot and environment are both quantum systems, with no link to classical robot hardware

Robotic task: Search of a two-dimensional region by a quantum robot
Method: Analysis of Grover-type search carried out by a quantum robot that must move through the region it searches
Key result: A quantum robot's Grover search of a two-dimensional region is no faster than a classical search, because the robot's motion cancels the query advantage
Limitation: Theoretical; assumes an idealized quantum robot

Method: Quantum robot architecture with multi-quantum computing units (MQCU), quantum controller/actuator and information acquisition units; Grover-based search and quantum reinforcement learning
Setup and data: Theoretical complexity analysis and simple learning simulations
Key result: Grover search lowers search complexity quadratically; simulated quantum RL learned more efficiently than a classical learner
Limitation: Assumes idealised on-board quantum hardware; small illustrative simulations

Robotic task: Multi-AGV collision-free routing in a factory
Method: Route selection for all AGVs posed as a QUBO with penalty terms for one-route-per-AGV and no simultaneous occupation of intersections; re-solved every time period
Setup and data: Simulation of a real DENSO plant layout with 10 AGVs (≤60 binary variables); D-Wave 2000Q, Fujitsu Digital Annealer and Gurobi compared with the conventional rule-based control
Key result: QUBO control gave smoother, collision-free traffic than the conventional rule; D-Wave produced plans in a short time but only for few vehicles; digital solvers handled larger instances quickly
Limitation: Small problem size on quantum hardware; post-processing needed to repair infeasible annealer outputs; classical solvers remained competitive or better

Quantum type: Quantum annealing (D-Wave, cloud) + classical and quantum-inspired solvers
Method: Real-time candidate-route generation, priority-weighted QUBO, and dynamic problem clustering that splits the fleet into sub-QUBOs; integrated with a commercial AGV operating system
Setup and data: Commercial AGV operating-system layout (154 m × 298 m, 8,242 tags) with real warehouse request data; AGV simulator with up to 1,000 AGVs
Key result: Route generation cut variables by 96% (small/medium) and 78% (large systems); clustering capped subproblems below 10,000 variables; complexity-based formulation reduced sampling time ~28%
Limitation: Fleet behavior simulated; no head-to-head speed comparison showing a quantum advantage over classical solvers

Method: Hybrid pipeline: classical computation generates candidate paths per robot; quantum annealing (QUBO) selects the conflict-free combination of paths
Setup and data: Grid-world routing benchmarked classically and on a D-Wave 2000Q with up to 200 robots
Key result: Valid (collision-free) multi-robot routing solutions obtained with current quantum annealing hardware for up to 200 robots
Limitation: Discrete grid; embedding and connectivity limits of the annealer; real-time claim not supported by end-to-end latency including cloud access

Method: AGV scheduling mapped to a railway-style scheduling model and solved with D-Wave hybrid (CQM) solvers
Setup and data: Realistic factory scenario, up to 21 AGVs and 7 zones (~1,300 variables); CPLEX baseline
Key result: Hybrid solver handled 21 AGVs in seconds and was comparable to classical solvers; AGV problems are sparser and better suited to QC than railway problems
Limitation: Proprietary hybrid solver, so the contribution of the QPU itself is unclear; CPLEX competitive

Quantum type: Quantum annealing hybrid (D-Wave) vs quantum-inspired (Fujitsu DA) vs classical (Gurobi)
Method: Three QUBO/MIP models of a transport-robot scheduling problem from a BASF high-throughput laboratory, benchmarked across solvers on end-to-end runtime and solution quality
Setup and data: Large instance set of varying difficulty; D-Wave hybrid, Fujitsu Digital Annealer (and hybrid), Gurobi
Key result: Gurobi reached comparable quality 10–100× faster on smaller instances; Fujitsu’s quantum-inspired hybrid was better on the largest instances; D-Wave showed only some opportunities
Limitation: Advantage, where found, came from quantum-inspired digital hardware rather than a quantum device

Robotic task: Warehouse order picking and batching for mobile robots
Quantum type: Quantum (VQE/QAOA and annealing via cloud; simulators)
Method: Picking/batching modeled as a capacitated vehicle-routing QUBO (docplex) and solved with VQE and other hybrid algorithms; robot controller on a Raspberry Pi 4 calling cloud QPUs
Setup and data: Proof of concept with small warehouse instances; IBM Q, Amazon Braket, D-Wave and PennyLane back-ends
Key result: Demonstrated an end-to-end robot-to-cloud quantum pipeline that returns valid routes for small instances
Limitation: Very small instances; no systematic comparison with classical VRP solvers; cloud latency not addressed for real-time use

Robotic task: Job scheduling for automated storage and retrieval systems
Quantum type: Quantum (QAOA on IBM Q System One)
Method: Scheduling formulated as an asymmetric QUBO and solved with QAOA
Setup and data: IBM Q System One (Ehningen); running time and qubit scalability study
Key result: Running time and qubit requirements quantified for small scheduling instances
Limitation: Small instances; scalability limited by qubit count

Robotic task: Industrial robot trajectory (sequencing) planning in automotive manufacturing
Quantum type: Quantum annealing (Amazon Braket, qbsolv) within a classical pipeline
Method: Biased random-key genetic algorithm with model stacking, ensembles and path relinking; quantum annealing complement via qbsolv on Amazon Braket
Setup and data: Industry-scale BMW data sets
Key result: Classical pipeline consistently outperformed greedy baselines; annealing results integrated as a quantum-ready module
Limitation: Nearly all of the performance comes from the classical algorithm; quantum hardware used only on reduced sub-problems

Method: Integer program reformulated as a QUBO and solved with a hybrid annealing workflow (QBSolv)
Setup and data: Small case: 4 tasks, 2 workstations, 2 equipment types
Key result: Optimal solutions found among samples, but total quantum workflow took ~10,110 s versus 0.03 s for the exact classical solver
Limitation: Toy instance; communication overhead dominates; connectivity and noise limit scale

Robotic task: Robotic quality-inspection path planning from CAD models
Quantum type: Quantum annealing hybrid (D-Wave CQM and NL solvers)
Method: Inspection trajectory modeled as a 3D open-route TSP on incomplete graphs; D-Wave hybrid solvers compared with Gurobi and Google OR-Tools
Setup and data: Five real industrial inspection cases
Key result: Competitive solution quality with significantly reduced computation time reported for the hybrid NL solver
Limitation: Short paper; hybrid solvers are proprietary; limited detail on runtimes

Method: Forward kinematics of each link encoded in a qubit via rotation gates, parent–child link coupling via entangling (RXX/RYY/RZZ) gates; joint angles optimized with classical COBYLA
Setup and data: Two-link manipulator with 3 rotational DOF per joint; Qiskit simulation and the RIKEN/Fujitsu 64-qubit superconducting computer
Key result: Adding entanglement reduced end-effector position error and sped up convergence, both in simulation and on hardware
Limitation: Only rotational joints; one-directional parent-to-child dependency; very small (2-qubit) problem; no comparison of accuracy or speed with classical IK solvers

Method: Planar IK reformulated as QUBO via linear binary discretization of joint angles with one-hot constraints; embedding strategies compared
Setup and data: Two-link planar IK instances on D-Wave Pegasus and Zephyr; classical QUBO baselines; rigorous time-to-solution
Key result: Global embedding on Zephyr used fewest qubits and shortest access time; hybrid solver had lower time-to-solution than classical QUBO baselines at larger sizes
Limitation: Authors explicitly do not claim superiority over continuous IK solvers; planar two-link case only

Robotic task: Regression testing of autonomous mobile robot software
Quantum type: Quantum (quantum reservoir computing, simulated) with industrial robot data
Method: QuReBot: quantum reservoir computing combined with a lightweight classical network to predict expected robot behavior as a test oracle
Setup and data: Industrial AMR data from PAL Robotics; classical neural-network baseline
Key result: QRC alone failed to converge; QuReBot converged and reduced prediction error (MSE) by ~15% versus the classical baseline
Limitation: Simulated quantum reservoir; single industrial robot and task

Quantum type: Quantum (simulated QCNN) with real driving data
Method: Fast quantum convolution that uploads input-channel information to cut qubit and circuit cost; quantum convolution-based object detection (QCOD)
Setup and data: KITTI autonomous-driving dataset; simulated quantum circuits
Key result: Object detection on KITTI with reduced computational complexity
Limitation: Simulated circuits; no on-vehicle or QPU deployment

Robotic task: Quantum robot interacting with a quantum target
Method: Quantum neural networks under a ’quantum force’ interpretation; quantum optimization of a conditional utility function for a quantum robot’s adaptive control
Setup and data: Examples on IBM’s five-qubit transmon chip via IBM Q Experience
Key result: Demonstrates implementability of small quantum neural networks and a quantum-robot control scheme on real hardware
Limitation: Highly theoretical; tiny circuits; no classical comparison

Method: Quantum-inspired RL (QiRL): action selection by ’collapse’ of an action superposition; amplitude-amplification-style reinforcement of good actions
Setup and data: 58-state Markov grid; 600×400-grid simulated navigation; real two-wheeled MT-R robot
Key result: Converged in ~2,000 episodes; more robust to learning rate and initial state than TD learning; learned obstacle avoidance faster than TD in simulation and on a real robot
Limitation: Runs entirely on a classical computer; compared only with basic TD learning; small discrete state spaces

Method: Hybrid quantum DDQN: parameterized quantum circuit (PQC) as Q-function approximator; two data-encoding schemes compared
Setup and data: Simulated Turtlebot 2 in three static grid environments and a large dynamic lidar environment; classical DDQN neural-network baseline
Key result: PQCs learned optimal policies with far fewer trainable parameters and beat parameter-matched classical networks; the larger classical network was faster, more stable and better in the dynamic environment
Limitation: Idealised noise-free simulation; no quantum hardware; advantage only when parameter counts are equalised

Method: DDPG with variational quantum circuits (horizontally shifting data re-uploading) as actor and critic; continuous wheel-velocity actions from LiDAR inputs
Setup and data: Simulated Turtlebot 2 in 3×3, 4×4 and 5×5 warehouse-like mazes; 4 and 8 qubits; classical DDPG (256×256) baseline
Key result: Best quantum model (8 qubits, 851 parameters) solved 3×3 and 4×4 mazes 30/30 but 5×5 only 10/30; classical DDPG (136,451 parameters) solved all 30/30; ~200× fewer parameters
Limitation: Classical baseline better on the hardest maze and in step efficiency; simulation only; more qubits/layers did not consistently help

Method: Nav-Q: actor–critic DRL in which the critic is a hybrid quantum–classical network; new QIDEP data-encoding extending data re-uploading
Setup and data: CARLA-CTS1.0 driving benchmark; classical NavA2C baseline; ideal and noisy quantum simulation
Key result: More stable training across initializations and sometimes faster convergence than NavA2C with far fewer parameters; higher effective dimension; noise degraded training but increased exploration
Limitation: Simulation only; quantum part used only in training (critic), so any benefit is to training, not to on-board inference

Method: Variational quantum Soft Actor-Critic (QSAC): actor and/or critics replaced by variational quantum circuits
Setup and data: Simulated robotic arm reaching task; classical SAC baselines with matched and 100× parameter counts
Key result: Fully quantum QSAC (~2,700 parameters) converged, whereas a classical SAC with ~3,000 parameters did not; classical SAC needed ~100× more parameters (~274k) to match
Limitation: Digital simulation only; single simple arm task; with a quantum actor alone there was no learning advantage; preprint

Method: Variational quantum soft actor-critic with parameterized quantum circuits
Setup and data: MuJoCo Walker2d-v4; classical SAC baseline; 17-qubit circuits in simulation
Key result: Quantum SAC reached ~8% higher average return than classical SAC with far fewer training steps, using 41 vs 1,250 learnable parameters
Limitation: Simulation only; Walker2d rather than full humanoid because of qubit limits; single environment

Method: Q-SpiRL: quantum-enhanced spiking neural network (QSNN) combining spike-based temporal processing with an 8-qubit variational circuit
Setup and data: 20×20, 30×30 and 40×40 grid worlds with static/dynamic obstacles; tabular Q-learning, MLP, SNN and quantum-MLP baselines
Key result: QSNN gave the best trade-off of success, path efficiency and smoothness, up to 99% success in the hardest setting; policy executed on IBM quantum hardware
Limitation: Discrete grid worlds; hardware run is a feasibility demonstration, not training on hardware; preprint

Method: CTDE multi-agent RL: variational quantum circuits for high-level policy exploration and spiking neural networks for low-latency control
Setup and data: Simulated forest environment with ten UAV agents, limited visibility and obstacles; classical MARL baselines
Key result: Fewer safety violations while maintaining exploration and interpretability, relative to classical MARL baselines
Limitation: Simulation only; lower-impact venue; quantum contribution not isolated from the SNN component

Robotic task: Cooperative mobile access with multi-UAV fleets
Method: Quantum multi-agent actor-critic networks with a quantum centralized critic
Setup and data: Simulated multi-UAV mobile-access environment; classical MARL baselines
Key result: Faster training and better wireless service quality than classical baselines with fewer parameters
Limitation: Simulated circuits and environment; communication-centric task

Method: Quantum MARL actor-critic with projection-value-measure action reduction
Setup and data: Simulated multi-agent mobility scenario
Key result: Parameter-efficient training and fast convergence; the projection-value measure reached the highest reward by reducing the action dimension to logarithmic scale
Limitation: Magazine-length evaluation; simulation only

Robotic task: Real-time balance control of a physical cart-pole
Quantum type: Quantum (simulated VQC) on physical control hardware
Method: Model-based offline policy search with a pure VQC policy (trainable input and output weights) in place of an MLP
Setup and data: Hardware cart-pole driven by a Raspberry Pi and an Arduino; VQC executed by local classical simulation; latency compared with IBM cloud execution
Key result: Quantum policies balanced the hardware cart-pole; local simulated execution met the real-time deadline, whereas cloud QPU execution took seconds
Limitation: Circuit simulated classically; single toy system; cloud QPU too slow for closed-loop control

Quantum type: Quantum (single-qubit VQC on the VTT Q5 superconducting QPU)
Method: Actor-critic policy gradient with a five-gate single-qubit variational circuit; readout electronics programmed directly through command tables
Setup and data: CartPole benchmark; VTT Q5 five-qubit processor with Zurich Instruments control electronics
Key result: Bypassing the standard software stack made circuit execution more than ten times faster; the single-qubit agent learned in fewer episodes than the classical baseline
Limitation: Throughput still below the tens of hertz needed for closed-loop control; one-qubit agent on a benchmark task

Method: Robot behavior encoded as a production system; plans found by Grover search over the action tree using a reversible Boolean oracle; qubit-reuse technique for simulation
Setup and data: Grid map with fixed obstacles; Qiskit Aer noiseless simulator on a 16 GB laptop (≈27-qubit limit)
Key result: Correct plans found with high success probability; quadratic reduction in search queries O(√N) versus exhaustive tree search
Limitation: Noise-free simulation only; qubits grow with plan depth; oracle construction assumes a known map; no comparison with classical planners such as A* or RRT

Method: Quantised position/reward information; pairwise information exchange as a quantum logic gate; per-robot Grover-based path planning (extends Chella et al., 2022)
Setup and data: Ant-foraging search-and-rescue scenario; Qiskit simulation; compared with NetLogo and Java ant-colony simulations
Key result: Faster convergence of the swarm to the target than both classical ant-behavior simulations
Limitation: Simulation only; small swarms; classical baselines are generic ant simulations rather than optimized swarm planners

Method: Sampling-based planners recast as database-oracle structures solved by quantum search, including quantum full path search (q-FPS) and quantum RRT (q-RRT)
Setup and data: Simulated planning problems (2D random lattices); q-RRT compared with classical RRT in classical simulation
Key result: Quadratic speed-up of q-RRT over RRT confirmed in simulation
Limitation: Speed-up shown only in classical simulation of the quantum algorithm; a real advantage needs fault-tolerant hardware

Method: Parameterized circuit trained to approximate forward kinematics, then used as a Grover oracle to search for optimal configurations
Setup and data: Simulated 1-DoF, 2-DoF and dual-arm manipulator tasks; Nelder-Mead and other classical optimizers as baselines
Key result: Quadratic reduction in search complexity; up to 93× speed-up over Nelder-Mead as dimensionality grew (simulated)
Limitation: Simulation only; speed-up counted in model evaluations/oracle queries rather than wall-clock time on hardware

Quantum type: Hybrid quantum ant-colony optimization (Qiskit simulation / Amazon Braket)
Method: Hybrid Quantum Ant Colony Optimization (HQACO): quantum circuits generate ant tours automatically from classical data, running ants in parallel on a hybrid architecture
Setup and data: TSPLIB instances and 50 random 16-node graphs; Qiskit simulator, Amazon Braket for larger circuits; OR-Tools optimum as reference
Key result: Optimal or near-optimal tours, with average error of about 7% from the optimum
Limitation: Simulated circuits; error grows with qubit count; no runtime advantage shown

Quantum type: Quantum (QUBO subproblems; real quantum hardware + classical)
Method: Branch-and-cut-and-price MAPF in which conflict-resolution subproblems are solved as QUBOs over conflict graphs (QUBO-and-Price, QUBO-Cut-and-Price)
Setup and data: Standard MAPF benchmarks; experiments on real quantum hardware; compared with BCP, EECBS, LaCAM* and LNS2
Key result: First optimal hybrid quantum–classical MAPF algorithms; outperformed earlier QUBO formulations and, on the reported benchmarks, state-of-the-art MAPF solvers
Limitation: Advantage depends on problem structure and small QUBO sizes; hardware results limited to small instances

Robotic task: UAV path planning with obstacle and no-fly-zone avoidance
Method: Pathfinding encoded as QAOA cost Hamiltonian with obstacle constraints and geospatial coordinate transformation
Setup and data: Simulations and a real-hardware run on IBM ibm_kyiv
Key result: Feasible, efficient trajectories generated despite hardware noise; circuit depth scales linearly with the number of graph edges
Limitation: Small graphs; no comparison of quality or runtime against classical planners such as A*

Quantum type: Quantum (QAOA via Eclipse Qrisp and D-Wave annealers)
Method: Two-phase Q4DR: QAOA-based clustering followed by annealer-based routing
Setup and data: Three use cases of increasing complexity with asymmetric costs, forbidden paths and charging points
Key result: Feasible routes for all three use cases
Limitation: Small use cases; quantum contribution not isolated from the classical decomposition

Robotic task: Multi-drone task assignment from natural-language instructions
Method: Fine-tuned LLM maps instructions to QUBO constraints; W-state initialization and XY mixers preserve assignment constraints; constraint-preserving partitioning with a separator-based dynamic-programming merge
Setup and data: Statevector simulation of decomposed sub-QUBOs
Key result: Global optimum in 100% of oracle evaluations and 96.3% of cases with CVaR-QAOA sampling
Limitation: Simulation only; hardware runs left to future work

Method: Objective function and constraint-preserving Quantum Alternating Operator Ansatz operators for exploring grid paths; validity proofs and resource estimation
Setup and data: 2D grid instances; comparison with depth-first search
Key result: Reported runtime improvements over DFS-based exploration; resource estimates for current hardware
Limitation: Theoretical/simulated; comparison against DFS rather than state-of-the-art coverage planners

Method: Joint QUBO for multiple robots with BFS-based variable pruning (>95% reduction) and time-windowed decomposition
Setup and data: Grids up to 10×10 with up to four robots; D-Wave simulated annealing and PennyLane-simulated QAOA
Key result: Near-optimal paths (5.3% length penalty in dense scenarios); classical planners remained faster at tested sizes
Limitation: No quantum hardware; small grids; single-author preprint

Method: Multi-term Hamiltonian for viewpoint selection with a parameter-centric variational ansatz using bidirectional alternating entanglement
Setup and data: Simulated exploration of diverse environments with obstacles; classical view-planning baselines
Key result: 7.9–49.2% higher exploration efficiency than classical methods; ablations attribute gains to entanglement structure
Limitation: Simulated quantum circuits; preprint; baselines not state-of-the-art NBV planners

Method: Localization cast as pattern search: the robot’s local perception costmap is matched against a pre-built map costmap with a Grover-search oracle
Setup and data: Small 2D grid maps; Qiskit simulation (≤40 qubits) and cloud quantum devices; compared with Monte Carlo localization (MCL)
Key result: Correct localization in simulation; theoretical O(√N) vs O(N) query scaling over map cells; accuracy on real devices degraded as map size grew
Limitation: Claimed speed-up is asymptotic query count, not measured wall-clock time; simulation capped at ~40 qubits; real-device noise limits map size; preprint

Method: Hybrid sensor: cold-atom matter-wave interferometer continuously corrects the bias drift of a classical accelerometer via a Kalman filter
Setup and data: Laboratory set-up with experimentally simulated harsh, mobile-like vibration environment
Key result: More precise and robust than sine-fitting; 400 Hz bandwidth with 10 ng stability after 11 h of integration
Limitation: Laboratory demonstration; single axis; size and power of cold-atom hardware remain barriers for mobile robots

Method: Three orthogonal atom interferometers hybridized with a navigation-grade classical accelerometer triad
Setup and data: Laboratory demonstration
Key result: Acceleration vector at 1 kHz with magnitude accuracy below 10 µg and 4 µrad pointing accuracy; 50-fold stability gain over classical accelerometers
Limitation: Laboratory set-up; not yet on a moving platform

Method: Maximum-likelihood probabilistic fusion that unwraps the phase of a cold-atom accelerometer using a co-located classical accelerometer, then recalibrates the classical sensor
Setup and data: Simulated 1D inertial navigation scenario
Key result: Extended the usable dynamic range of the quantum accelerometer and reduced navigation error compared with classical-only sensing
Limitation: 1D simulation only; fusion errors when phase ambiguity is large

Method: Diamond (NV-center) magnetometer measurements with probabilistic data association and multiple-hypothesis/Viterbi map-matching filters to aid an IMU
Setup and data: Simulations at current and near-term diamond magnetometer sensitivities; scalar and vector magnetometry
Key result: Quantifies expected navigation errors and shows vector diamond magnetometry can bound INS drift
Limitation: Simulation only; depends on magnetic anomaly map quality

Method: Magnetic-anomaly navigation using proprietary quantum magnetometers plus denoising and map-matching algorithms that learn platform parameters online
Setup and data: Flight trials from ground level to ~19,000 ft with onboard/outboard sensors; ground-vehicle trial with public anomaly maps; strategic-grade INS as comparator
Key result: Up to ~46× lower positioning error than a velocity-aided strategic-grade INS (best final error 22 m, 0.006% of distance); ≥11× better across airborne trials; ~7× better in the ground vehicle
Limitation: Company-led preprint (Q-CTRL); depends on quality of magnetic-anomaly maps; periodic fixes rather than continuous high-rate positioning

Method: Photon-based quantum capabilities (SPDC single photons, polarisation, single-photon detection, entanglement and cryptography concepts) integrated into networks of classical aerial and ground robots
Setup and data: Laboratory demonstrations on classical aerial and ground robotic platforms
Key result: Shows the feasibility of carrying quantum-optical communication hardware on cooperating robots
Limitation: Conceptual/laboratory scale; no quantitative performance comparison

Quantum type: Quantum communication (field experiment on a drone)
Method: Compact polarisation-encoded decoy-state BB84 QKD transmitter on an octocopter
Setup and data: Drone (≤30 kg take-off weight) to ground over 200 m
Key result: Real-time QKD with an average secret-key rate of 8.48 kHz
Limitation: Short range; single drone; focus on communication rather than autonomy

Method: Entangled-photon source on one drone and an optical relay on a second drone
Setup and data: Drone-to-drone relayed link over 1 km
Key result: Entanglement distribution at 1 km with CHSH S = 2.59 ± 0.11
Limitation: above the classical bound
DOI or identifier: Short range; no robotic task built on the link

Robotic task: Secure communication between drones and ground vehicles
Quantum type: Quantum communication (field deployment on moving platforms)
Method: Modular, platform-agnostic, reduced-SWaP QKD transmitter and receiver with device models for mobile non-idealities
Setup and data: Drone-to-drone, drone-to-vehicle and vehicle-to-vehicle links
Key result: Finite-key secure key rates of 1.6–20 kbps between moving platforms
Limitation: Communication only; ranges and conditions limited

Quantum type: Quantum cognition model on quantum hardware
Method: Quantum-probability cognitive models (question-order effects, decisions under uncertainty) implemented as small qubit circuits with gates and measurements
Setup and data: Circuits run on an 11-qubit IonQ trapped-ion computer and simulators
Key result: Very small circuits (some a single qubit) reproduce human order effects and non-classical decision patterns
Limitation: Models are small enough to simulate classically, so no computational advantage is claimed; not applied to robots

Robotic task: Robot emotion modeling / multi-robot emotion fusion
Method: Emotions encoded as qubit superposition states in an emotion space; unitary operators model emotion transitions; entanglement fuses the emotions of multiple robots
Setup and data: Mathematical framework with small simulation-based demonstrations
Key result: Entanglement-based fusion reduces the qubits and gates needed to represent and update the joint emotional state of a robot group
Limitation: Conceptual; no psychological validation, no physical robots, no comparison with classical affective models

Method: Literature review (>35 articles, 2021–2025) and project proposal for quantum-enhanced HRI
Key result: Identifies emotion recognition, path finding and cognitive modeling as candidate uses of Grover search and quantum walks in social robots
Limitation: Short position paper; no implementation or evaluation yet

Quantum type: Quantum algorithms in a cognitive architecture (simulated)
Method: Prefrontal-cortex-inspired cognitive architecture with transformer-based RL and quantum routines (Deutsch–Jozsa, Bernstein–Vazirani, Grover) for decision-making, meta-cognition and situation awareness
Setup and data: Minecraft-based simulation environment with multi-objective exploration tasks
Key result: About 2× faster convergence to 80% task success and ~15% higher cumulative reward than the classical agent
Limitation: Simulated circuits; game environment; the role of each quantum routine is not isolated

Method: Quantum-like interdependence theory: team states are non-separable (entangled-like), and measuring individuals cannot reconstruct team performance
Key result: Argues that interdependence, not individual aggregation, explains team performance under complexity, uncertainty and conflict
Limitation: Theoretical; no quantitative robot experiments

Method: Quantum probability theory applied to human rationalisation of AI outputs (order and interference effects, ontic uncertainty)
Setup and data: Illustrative case study
Key result: Shows how QPT predicts oscillating, order-dependent beliefs that classical models miss
Limitation: Perspective paper; not robot-specific; no empirical test

Method: Multi-player, multi-strategy quantum game combining classical game theory with superposed and entangled strategies
Setup and data: Simulated interactive driving scenarios; classical game-theoretic baselines
Key result: Higher success rates and fewer collisions than classical approaches, especially in highly interactive scenarios
Limitation: Simulation only; no human-in-the-loop or vehicle tests

Method: QPSO-FastSLAM: quantum-behaved particle swarm optimization (with Gaussian disturbance) refines the particle proposal distribution; diversity-triggered linear-optimization resampling
Setup and data: Bailey’s FastSLAM simulator (90 m × 70 m, 18 landmarks, 20 Monte Carlo runs); Victoria Park outdoor data set
Key result: Lower pose and landmark RMSE than FastSLAM 2.0 and PSO-FastSLAM (e.g., 0.44 m vs 0.52 m with 20 particles); same accuracy with fewer particles
Limitation: Runs on classical hardware (quantum-inspired only); compared only with FastSLAM variants

Robotic task: Inverse kinematics of a 6-DoF industrial arm
Method: Multi-layer perceptrons with a quantum-inspired activation function, compared with classical ANNs
Setup and data: ABB IRB140 model (DH parameters) in RobotStudio; singularity-free and singularity-avoidance data sets
Key result: 15.6–16.7% lower mean absolute error than classical ANNs; 1.64 mm position and 0.00179 rad orientation accuracy
Limitation: Despite the name, no quantum hardware or circuit; runs entirely classically

Method: Category-theoretic classification of swarms and a block-matrix model whose off-diagonal (pairwise) terms are computed with a 4-qubit circuit
Setup and data: Toy model run in IBM Quantum Composer on simulators and real IBM quantum computers
Key result: Worked example linking local pairwise quantum interactions to global swarm behavior
Limitation: Toy model; no performance comparison

Method: Pairwise robot interactions encoded as a quantum circuit with a custom logic gate; block-matrix model linking local (diagonal) and pairwise (off-diagonal) terms to global swarm behavior
Setup and data: Toy swarms of 3 and 10 robots in an ant-foraging scenario; quantum simulators and quantum computers
Key result: Shows emergence of global foraging behavior from quantum pairwise interactions and analyzes the effect of entanglement
Limitation: Explicitly not an optimization method; very small swarms; no comparison of efficiency

Method: Local-to-global framework: pairwise quantum circuits (e.g., XNOR-type decision gates) inside classical swarm algorithms; Grover-based path planning; sonification of swarm motion
Setup and data: Webots robot simulator coupled to the Qiskit simulator; 2D/3D arenas, search-and-rescue and aquatic-robot scenarios
Key result: Quantum pairwise-interaction swarms reported to converge faster and travel less than classical counterparts in simulation
Limitation: Simulation only; file-exchange latency between simulators; on-board quantum computers infeasible on small robots, so an external computing center is required

Method: Swarm described as a mixed quantum state (density matrix) whose dimension does not grow with the number of robots
Setup and data: Theoretical proposal
Key result: Size-invariant representation of swarm state; research directions
Limitation: No implementation or evaluation
